newsitem.title: FINLAND: Private sector sees opportunities in Nordic countries.
newsitem.headline: Private sector sees opportunities in Nordic countries.

text.p: Public welfare provision in Nordic countries is being increasingly stretched by growing numbers of the unemployed and the retired, but private providers are eager to meet increasing demand for pensions from a relatively well-off population.
Though the pensions system is very different in each country, many private or market-led providers see the question of funding commitments to the year 2020 as an opportunity rather than headache.

Reform of public pension schemes is high on the agenda -- especially in Sweden, where the state's role in insurance is biggest -- but the issue is a political hot potato and many far-reaching issues have yet to be faced.

With the Nordic welfare model increasingly under fire in competitive world markets, insurance company executives say mere talk of the need to shore up statutory collective pension schemes is fuelling demand for individual top-up policies.

Also clear is a trend among schemes which are based on funds -- a significant slice of statutory entitlements is contribution-funded -- to boost the risk component of their portfolios and look further afield for better returns.

It is hard to get an overview of the total they have to invest, but data collected by Reuters from diverse sources suggest that there is at least $340 billion in both public and private Nordic pension-related assets.

Most of this will remain in the region, bound in many cases to match growing liabilities in local currency. But Danish and Swedish funds, particularly, are directing a larger share of hitherto bond-heavy portfolios to equities and property.

As demand patterns shift, boosting individual schemes to supplement collective agreements built up after the 1960s, risk components like stocks rise. And given their relatively small home economies, Nordic funds are looking abroad more.
Mogens Joergensen of the executive board at top Danish insurer Danica, the country's second largest pension provider with about 120 billion Danish crowns to invest, is succinct.
"I don't know where we should buy the bonds from," he said, referring to Denmark's decreasing borrowing requirement.

Official statistics from the four countries point to a clear increase in the burden of pensioners on the population by the year 2020, although in some countries the real "greying" starts to grow more dramatically after then.
Calculations vary, but data collected by Reuters suggests about 22 percent on average of the Nordic population will be claiming pensions in 2020, against 19 percent now.
Finland looks set to continue to have the region's oldest population, Denmark the youngest.

Sweden does not serve as a model for the other Nordic countries' pension schemes -- the state has the weightiest role there -- but it stands out as having the toughest problem with future commitments.

Sweden's ATP national pension scheme, which provides the lion's share of the pay-out individuals currently receive, is having to use an increasingly large share of its buffer fund to cover its pension payments.

As part of continuing reforms, Finance Minister Erik Asbrink has said the law governing the six AP funds which back up the ATP will be examined by the summer, but there are no changes proposed yet and much remains unclear.

In Denmark, where the government also pays a basic pension, proposals to defer the public pensionable age -- or scrap early retirement -- have roused heated controversy among a population looking to quit work sooner rather than later.
Danes already face rising contributions to their top-up funds. The biggest single provider, also called ATP, was set up by social legislation but aims to function as any insurer.

In Norway, the wealth generated by oil revenues makes for a brighter overall picture and in Finland, where statutory, private pension schemes already play a central role, reform so far has focussed on relaxing investment curbs.

Overall, public schemes still cater for the lion's share of the Nordic "social security market", according to a report published by the Nordic insurance associations last year to highlight their potential in some parts of that market.

The report showed private insurers in 1992 had just a 16 percent share of all claims paid out. Their role was smallest in Sweden -- at 11 percent -- and highest in Finland at 26 percent. Swedish insurers say little has changed since.
Insurance payouts make up about one-third of Gross National Product in the four Nordic countries, the report said.
The economies of Denmark, Norway and Sweden rank in the global top 10 by Gross Domestic Product per head and Finland is in the top 20.
"Payments from public schemes are more than five times greater than those from private schemes," the report said.
"Even a small shift from public to private sector insurance schemes will produce a large increase in business for the insurance companies and pension funds," it added.
Sweden's SPP, a mutual life insurance company, said in 1995 that about 70 percent of the Swedish life insurance market was open to competition, a share which would keep growing until 2000.

"During this period the life insurance market is expected to grow to more than 90 billion Swedish crowns, an increase of approximately 30 billion. The main part of this growth will occur in the occupational pension sector...," SPP said.

For some years, regulators have been increasing the scope for pension-providers to boost the risk component of their portfolios and generate fatter yields -- Finland was the most recent, but retains a relatively conservative profile.
The limits are defined in different ways, but roughly about one-third of funds' total assets can go into equities, with the tightest restrictions in Finland and the loosest in Denmark.
Overseas exposure is generally capped around 20 percent, and many funds now keep only about 10 percent in foreign currencies.
Rolf Nordstrand, fund director at Denmark's ATP, which has about 150 billion Danish crowns to invest and at end-1995 held about 30 percent in equities, had a fairly typical view.
"There is a trend towards stocks," he said, expecting ATP to hit its own 35 percent limit in equities "fairly soon".
ATP started investing overseas about six years ago and now has about seven percent exposure, with an official ceiling at 10 percent but an actual one widely seen nearer 20 percent.
Most fund managers contacted said they felt comfortable with existing limits -- for instance ATP can but does not use derivatives for hedging -- but saw bottlenecks further ahead.
For instance in Finland, Kari Puro, leader of a group which laid down plans for reform and who is head of key pension provider Ilmarinen, said the system will need reviewing again quite soon.
"In this situation ... I imagine we can live for approximately the next five years but after that, the whole system should be considered again," he said.
